https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1e1.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, It is the second school shooting in the Philippines in as many months By Joel Guinto Published 8 hours ago A student at a Catholic junior high school in the southern Philippines was shot dead by a fellow student, who later took his own life, a local official said on Tuesday. The alleged shooter managed to sneak in a .45-calibre pistol into a classroom at the school in Zamboanga City, Mayor Khymer Adan Olaso told local radio. The suspect fired at the teacher who was seated at the table, but missed. Afterwards, the suspect moved to another classroom and shot a student who later died, Olaso said. Alleged livestream footage of the shooting, circulated by local media, showed what appeared to be a first-person perspective, with a gun barrel moving down a hallway, AFP News Agency reported. The situation was under control and there were no more active shooters, authorities said. The incident comes two months after a high school shooting in Tacloban City in the central region left three students killed and 20 others wounded. The suspects in that shooting were two teenage boys, one of whom was found to have regularly played an explicitly violent online game. The sandbox game, Gorebox, has been banned in the Philippines and the Senate is investigating the effects of violent computer games on young people. Across South East Asia, authorities are looking at restricting social media use for minors, citing possible ill effects. Earlier this month, a Thai teenager killed eight people and himself at his school. Authorities said he consumed violent content on social media . https://www.moneycontrol.com/world/cia-c.text: Donald Trump H1B Visa News Iran Missile Attack Strait of Hormuz US Midterm Elections CIA chief’s secret Moscow trip: Trump’s three messages to Russia, even top officials were unaware CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s secret Moscow trip reportedly carried three key messages from Donald Trump, don’t attack NATO, end the Ukraine war and distance Russia from Iran. Moneycontrol World Desk August 29, 2026 / 15:10 IST Trump sent CIA chief on secret Moscow mission with three messages for Russia US President Donald Trump sent CIA Director John Ratcliffe on a secret mission to Moscow this week, where he delivered messages on NATO, the war in Ukraine and Russia’s ties with Iran, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal. Ratcliffe travelled to the Russian capital on Tuesday for meetings with senior Russian intelligence officials, though he did not meet President Vladimir Putin, officials familiar with the visit said. The mission was reportedly kept secret even from some senior White House and military officials. Ratcliffe travelled from Latvia to Moscow aboard an unmarked US C-17 military cargo aircraft, according to The WSJ. CIA chief’s three messages to Moscow During the meeting, Ratcliffe urged Russian officials not to attack NATO countries, to work towards ending the war in Ukraine and to reconsider their economic and security ties with Iran, according to sources familiar with the discussions. The CIA director also reiterated Washington’s commitment to NATO’s Article 5, under which an attack on one member of the alliance is treated as an attack on all members. The message came amid growing concerns among European officials about Russia’s military intentions and intelligence assessments suggesting Moscow could seek to test NATO’s resolve in the coming years. Trump, however, sought to downplay fears of a Russian attack on the alliance, saying Putin "won't attack NATO territory." Ukraine war remained central to talks The war in Ukraine was the main focus of Ratcliffe’s discussions in Moscow, according to officials familiar with the matter. The CIA chief reportedly pressed Russian officials to revive negotiations aimed at ending the conflict after previous diplomatic efforts by members of the Trump administration failed to produce a breakthrough. Kyrylo Budanov, chief of Ukraine’s presidential office, said on Thursday that negotiations could resume in September. Ratcliffe’s trip marked another attempt by Trump to open a channel with Moscow after earlier efforts involving special envoy Steve Witkoff and other senior administration figures failed to secure an agreement. The White House has described Ratcliffe’s visit as “semi-routine." The CIA declined to comment on the trip. Russia’s ties with Iran also raised Ratcliffe also discussed Russia’s relationship with Iran during the Moscow meetings, reports said. The CIA chief urged Russian officials to avoid maintaining economic and security ties with Tehran as the Trump administration intensifies pressure on Iran. The issue comes against the backdrop of closer cooperation between Moscow and Tehran, including reports of Russian supplies of drone components, ammunition and explosives to Iran through the Caspian Sea. Why Trump turned to Ratcliffe Ratcliffe’s longstanding intelligence channels with Russian officials and his position within Trump’s inner circle were among the reasons behind his selection for the sensitive mission, according to officials cited by The Wall Street Journal. He has also previously dealt with Russian authorities and helped secure the release of American hostages. J.C. Lintzenich, a former senior US intelligence official and national security adviser in the Senate, said Ratcliffe’s personal delivery of the message was intended to make clear that Trump's push for peace in Ukraine would not come at the expense of Washington's commitments to Europe. “Putin has a tolerance for extraordinary risk and is even potentially willing to escalate to compel de-escalation, but he is unlikely to roll the dice on actions that could threaten the Russian state," said Lintzenich. Europe watches Russia’s next moves Ratcliffe’s visit comes as European governments remain concerned about what they describe as an escalating Russian hybrid campaign against countries backing Ukraine. Officials have pointed to incidents involving drones, missile threats, cyberattacks and explosive packages as signs of efforts to undermine European support for Kyiv and create divisions within NATO. Some European officials are particularly focused on the period around 2030, when Russia’s military could recover from losses sustained in Ukraine while European nations are still strengthening their own defence capabilities. Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs sought to ease concerns on Thursday, saying, "There is currently no reason for concern," while adding that "Latvia's level of military threat hasn't changed. The risk of direct military invasion threats to Latvia is currently low." The Moscow mission, however, underlined Washington’s attempt to use intelligence channels alongside diplomacy as it seeks movement on Ukraine while managing rising tensions involving Russia, NATO and Iran. https://apollo-magazine.com/lonnie-bunch.text: Lonnie G. Bunch III to step down as head of the Smithsonian By Apollo, 11 September 2026 Apollo 11 September 2026 News Lonnie G. Bunch III, Secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, speaks at an event at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C., in February 2026. Photo: Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images Lonnie G. Bunch III is retiring as secretary of the Smithsonian Institution after seven years in the role. He is the first historian – and the first Black person – to have been made head of the institution. He arrived from the Smithsonian’s National Museum of African American History and Culture, of which he was the founding director; in 2005 he secured $250m from Congress to help establish the museum. The Smithsonian has come under intense pressure from the White House during the current Trump administration. Last year the government launched a review into the institution, which remains ongoing, and threatened to withdraw the Smithsonian’s funding – which makes up 62 per cent of its budget – if the institution did not comply with the terms of the review. Bunch told the New York Times that the pressure from the Trump administration ‘has been stressful’, but that this was not the reason for his departure. ‘It was really just saying [that] now’s the time,’ he said. Two paintings by Pierre-Auguste Renoir have been stolen from the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer in the French Riviera, the BBC reports . Two thieves entered by cutting a hole in a fence and grabbed four works but abandoned two, Portrait de Madame Pichon (1895) and Coco lisant (1905), on their way out. Jeune femme au puits (1886) and Portrait de Madame Colonna Romano (1910), with an estimated joint value of €9m, are still missing. According to the Association for Research into Crimes Against Art , Jeune femme au puits was once owned by the Jewish art dealer Hedwig Zak before being sold under duress to another Parisian dealer and later seized by the Nazis; Zak and her son were killed at Birkenau. Le Monde reports that Zak’s heirs have demanded the painting’s return. French museums have been hit by a number of heists in the last year: crown jewels at the Louvre last October, a gold torc dating to c . 500 BC from the Musée du Pays Châtillonnais in Burgundy in July and €4.5m-worth of jewellery from the Musée Lalique in north-east France, also in July. The mayor’s office in Cagnes-sur-Mer has said that ‘every possible effort’ is being made to find those responsible for the latest theft. Anti-migrant protestors in Dorset have caused the Poole Old Lifeboat Museum to temporarily close, the BBC reports . Protestors gathered in Poole after some 140 migrants arrived on a dinghy from France last week. According to a Facebook post by the museum, which is free and run by volunteers, the protestors were ‘verbally assaulting’ volunteers ‘in and around the museum’ making it impossible to open the museum. The museum, which documents the history of the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI) in Poole since 1865, also stated that it would remain shut until the protests ended. The Hungarian government has scrapped plans for a new National Gallery building in Budapest, the Art Newspaper reports . In 2011 Géza Szőcs, the then culture secretary in Viktor Orbán’s government, announced plans to create a museum quarter in City Park, with a new building that would house Hungarian and international art made after 1800. In 2015 the Japanese firm SANAA was hired to design the €300m building but the project stalled in 2019 due to opposition from the mayor of Budapest and environmental groups. Now, under the new government led by Péter Magyar, the planned building site will revert to public parkland. Dávid Vitézy, minister of transport and public works, told the Art Newspaper that, though the City Park is no longer a viable option, the National Gallery’s current location – Buda castle, on the other side of the Danube – falls short of ‘the standards required for the long-term operation of a modern national art gallery’, and that the government ‘must develop a new plan for the future location of the Hungarian National Gallery’. An Argentine court has ordered that a Nazi-looted painting by Giacomo Ceruti be returned to the heir of the Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker, the Art Newspaper reports . Portrait of a Lady , which dates to the 18th century and was previously attributed to Giuseppe Ghislandi, was discovered in photographs from a property listing in the resort city of Mar del Plata. The home belonged to the descendants of a Nazi official who fled Europe after the Second World War. Goudstikker died in 1940 trying to flee the Netherlands after the Germans invaded; the Nazis looted his gallery of more than 1,100 works. His heir, Marei von Saher, told the Art Newspaper that he hopes the painting can be exhibited publicly in Argentina before its restitution. The Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford will repatriate the remains of 39 people to the Naga community in north-eastern India. The Naga community has been negotiating for the return of the remains, which mostly comprise skulls, for more than six years, since around the time that the museum took all its human remains off display. The remains were donated in the early 20th century by the colonial administrators John Henry Hutton and James Philip Mills. According to the museum, Mills, on a punitive exhibition in 1936, ‘recorded demanding heads from a village and waiting with an armed escort until they were produced’. The requested remains of one other person will remain at the museum because, in the museum’s words, it ‘does not have a clear provenance as Naga’. The Pitt Rivers retains 178 Naga objects that contain or may contain human hair.
